messages.subject: Re: Stepwise regression in geomorph
parts:
Dear Alexandre,

I am cc’ing the geomorph google group in this response because it is a question that I think is intriguing for our community.

There are multiple ways to answer this question, but the simplest is no, there is no way to use the step or stepAIC functions on geomorph objects.  Inherent in those functions is the extracAIC function, which can be applied to objects of class lm, glm, aov, etc.  These are all univariate.  Why? I am not sure but suspect its because in order to calculate AIC, one needs to calculate log-likelihoods, and in order to calculate log-likelihoods for multivariate data, one must find the determinant of the residual covariance matrix.  That last part is troublesome if covariance matrices are singular, which is so likely with GM data that we might as well consider it a certainty for a function.  So there is no reliable way to extend geomorph to these other multi-use functions, unless we redefine how to calculate AIC with highly multivariate data, an area of research is strong need of theoretical development.

Alternatively, we could use a different criterion than AIC in a stepwise procedure.  Older methods use P-values and define a criterion, like P < 0.25 to keep terms.  We could possibly create something like this for procD.lm objects, but one would have to define a number of permutations, and every model comparison would require waiting for say, 1000 permutations to run.  Set it up before you go to sleep and get the results in the morning, and try not to be burdened by the inelegance of using P-values (I will not go into the many reasons this is ill-advised here).  This just does not seem worth creating.

So, a stepwise procedure — which I would love to have — is still in the “maybe in the future” stage at this point.

We do have a function in RRPP called model.comparison, that could use separate procD.lm fits (same as lm.rrpp fits) to graphically show the trace of residual covariance matrix or -2 *log-likelihood versus parameter penalty (like is calculated in AIC).  This is descriptive (so is AIC) but is diagnostically helpful.  The only problem is you would have to estimate many models first to compare them (the examples in the help file should be informative for how to set it up).

I might have to think if I can add an algorithm for a stepwise option to this in the future.  I’m not sure it is possible.  But if you are willing to fit several models, you can compare them to find which has the lowest error compared to the expected error based on the number of parameters; i.e., a form of model selection.  I think it is the best option we have for shape data at the moment.

I hope this is helpful, even if the news is disappointing.

Cheers!
Mike

On May 7, 2020, at 3:35 PM, Alexandre Ferreira <alexandr...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Mike,

I hope this email finds you well.

My name is Alexandre, I recently started working with geometric morphometrics and I'm facing a problem with models selection.

I'm working with 3D GM in ants. My focus is on understanding how the mandible and head shape vary within and between workers in the ant genus Pheidole. Also, I want to test how these parts are integrated, and how behavioral factors influence these features. 

For this, I complied a 3D model database of Pheidole workers, for a total of 27 species. Therefore, I categorized their feeding behavior as granivorous, non-granivorous, or unknown, and their nesting habits as soil, twigs, or unknown. 

To assess the influence of the ecological factors on the shape patterns I used linear models of shape variation. For this, I performed a Procrustes ANOVA considering a residual randomization permutation procedure and contrasting the linear models. In total, I generated five relevant models, first considering the isolated effect of the size, food preference, and nesting habitat on the shape; then for the interaction between size and food preference, as well as for size and nesting habitat. To run my models I followed the "Addition by Subtraction: Improving geomorph with fewer functions" examples that you made available. 

looking like this:

gdf.s.mand<-geomorph.data.frame(mand.shape = mand.s.gpa$coords,
                                mand.size = mand.s.gpa$Csize,
                                pref = class.mand.s$Pref,
                                nidf = class.mand.s$Nidf)

fit.s.mand.model.1<-procD.lm(mand.shape~
                               mand.size+
                               pref+
                               nidf+
                               mand.size*pref+
                               mand.size*nidf,
                             data = gdf.s.mand, print.progress = F)

anova(fit.s.mand.model.1)


Now I'm trying to perform a stepwise selection. I've been struggling to use the function stepAIC from the MASS package, however, it's doesn't seem to work. 

I wonder if you have any suggestions that I can follow to make my model selection? Is there any function that I can apply using the geomorph package? I confess that I didn't find anything, but I apologize if it was my misinterpretation of some function of the package. 

I would like to thank you in advance for your attention.

I hope that you stay safe and healthy in these terrible times that we're living,

Best wishes,

Ale
